issues.description: The problem statement and UML specify Rideable.messageOnRide() with no parameters (returns String), and the template Main example calls r.messageOnRide() without arguments. The solution, however, defines Rideable.messageOnRide(int speed) and implements messageOnRide(int) in Pig and Seal. This parameter mismatch between specification/template and the provided solution will confuse students about the intended interface signature and cause compilation mismatch if they follow the problem statement or the solution inconsistently.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the Rideable.messageOnRide signature consistent across all artifacts. Either: (A) update the problem statement, UML, and template examples to specify messageOnRide(int speed) and show example calls with a speed argument; or (B) modify the solution to implement messageOnRide() with no parameters (and adjust Pig/Seal implementations accordingly). Ensure the UML and Main example match the chosen signature.

issues.description: The problem statement and template expect a no-argument method messageOnRide() (signature: messageOnRide():String), but the solution defines Rideable.messageOnRide(int speed) and implementations (Pig, Seal) implement messageOnRide with an int parameter. This mismatch in the method signature for the same conceptual operation (producing the ride message) creates confusion: students are instructed and scaffolded to call messageOnRide() with no arguments (see Main.java in the template and the textual task), while the reference solution requires an int parameter. This breaks the mapping between requirements, template usage, and the solution implementation.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the method signature consistent across all artifacts. Either (A) change the solution to match the problem/template by declaring Rideable.messageOnRide() with no parameters and update Pig/Seal implementations to return "Riding on [Animal Type] [name]" (remove the speed parameter), or (B) update the problem statement and template to specify messageOnRide(int speed) and adjust example calls (e.g., r.messageOnRide(5)). Aligning to one signature will remove the conceptual mapping burden for students.
